title: Salve Regina

lines: THE LONG GREEN STRETCH: ORDINARY TIME.
cards: A valley of tears. A strange address to put in a prayer, and an honest one. After Easter and Pentecost, the Church settles into the long green stretch of the year it calls Ordinary Time.
Just Mondays, laundry, work, a sick parent, a good dinner, a bad night. For that stretch, the song at the end of night prayer is the one that knows exactly where people live.
It opens with a greeting, hail, holy queen, and before it's done it has named exile, sighing, mourning and weeping. You first met it on day one hundred twenty-three. Today, it goes slowly.

teach.h: MOTHER OF MERCY, OUR LIFE, OUR HOPE.
teach.b: It moves in four steps. First, names: Salve Regina, mater misericordiae. Hail, queen, mother of mercy, our life, our sweetness and our hope.
Second, the truth about where the singers stand.

teach.h: EXILED CHILDREN OF EVE, IN TEARS.
teach.b: To you we cry, exiled children of Eve; to you we send up our sighs, mourning and weeping in this valley of tears. A few days ago Mary was the new Eve, who untied the knot.
Here the singers call themselves Eve's children, still far from home. The prayer doesn't pretend that ordinary life is easy. It names the tears and keeps singing.
Turn your eyes of mercy toward us, it asks, and after this exile, show us Jesus, the blessed fruit of your womb.

That phrase comes from Elizabeth's greeting in Luke's Gospel, which the Douay-Rheims gives as "blessed is the fruit of thy womb." Notice what the prayer asks: not for Mary to stand in for her son, but to show him.
The whole song leans toward him. Fourth, three last cries: O clemens, O pia, O dulcis Virgo Maria.

teach.h: O CLEMENT, O LOVING, O SWEET.
teach.b: O clement, O loving, O sweet Virgin Mary.

teach.h: BLESSED IS THE FRUIT OF THY WOMB.
teach.b: A story links those last cries to Saint Bernard of Clairvaux; it isn't certain.
Either way, the song ends not with an argument but with a sigh of affection, on an ordinary night, in an ordinary valley, with the lights about to go out.

how: Catholics sing or say the Salve Regina at the end of Night Prayer in Ordinary Time, and it is also prayed at the end of the rosary; some religious communities sing it together in chant before the night's silence.

o: Latin for a farewell sung at a queen's funeral
Latin for hail, queen: the night song of ordinary days
Latin for safe travels, said to pilgrims

p: where the prayer says we are

s: the Salve Regina pretends life is easy
it names exile, sighing, mourning and weeping in a valley of tears.
it asks Mary to show us Jesus
after this exile, show us the blessed fruit of your womb, Jesus.
it's proven that Saint Bernard wrote the last three cries
that's a story people tell. it isn't certain.

games.q: you're writing a song for the ordinary weeks of the year: no feast, just life. how honest do you get about sadness?
o: keep it cheerful. people need lifting.
name the exile, the sighing and the weeping out loud.
games.why: the Salve Regina names exile, mourning and weeping in a valley of tears, and then asks to be shown Jesus.

practice: Name honestly one thing in your valley right now, then one sweetness that's also true, a person, a small joy, a reason for hope, and hold the two side by side, the way the prayer does.
If you pray, say or sing the Salve Regina, from hail, holy queen to O sweet Virgin Mary; if you don't, name the same two again, one tear, one hope.
If the valley ever feels too dark to bear, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

wordCard.voice: Salve Regina. Hail, holy queen: the night song of Ordinary Time, honest about the valley of tears, asking to be shown Jesus.
